differential: Vestibular Schwannoma
This benign tumor classically presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and disequilibrium due to compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
Meniere's Disease
This inner ear disorder is characterized by the triad of fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo, which can become chronic over time.
Meningioma
A tumor in the cerebellopontine angle can compress the vestibulocochlear nerve, mimicking the symptoms of a vestibular schwannoma.
Cholesteatoma
This destructive growth in the middle ear can cause hearing loss and dizziness, and may erode into the inner ear to produce these specific symptoms.
Autoimmune Inner Ear Disease
A systemic inflammatory condition can target the inner ear, causing progressive sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction.
eliminated: Presbycusis
The patient's age of 23 makes age-related hearing loss extremely unlikely.
Cerebrovascular Accident
A stroke would present with a sudden onset of symptoms, not a progressive course over six months.
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
This condition causes isolated, brief episodes of vertigo without the associated hearing loss or tinnitus.
Acute Otitis Media
This is an acute infection and would not cause chronic symptoms over a six-month period.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)

The combination of bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and bilateral facial weakness in a young adult is the classic presentation for bilateral vestibular schwannomas characteristic of this diagnosis.
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX)
This diagnosis is suggested by the combination of neurological dysfunction (ataxia, cranial nerve deficits) and xanthomatous skin lesions.
Neurosarcoidosis
This systemic inflammatory condition is a strong consideration as it can cause multiple cranial neuropathies (especially bilateral facial palsy), ataxia, and skin papules/plaques.
Erdheim-Chester disease
This rare histiocytosis can present with CNS infiltration causing ataxia and cranial nerve palsies, as well as xanthomatous skin lesions.
Refsum disease
This metabolic disorder presents with sensorineural hearing loss and ataxia, though the described skin lesions are less typical than the ichthyosis usually seen.
eliminated: Meniere's disease
This condition would not explain the bilateral facial weakness or the cutaneous findings.
Unilateral vestibular schwannoma
The presence of bilateral facial muscle weakness makes a single unilateral lesion highly unlikely.
Multiple sclerosis
This demyelinating disease does not account for the presence of yellow skin plaques and papules.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2
The presence of bilateral masses in the cerebellopontine angles, highly suggestive of vestibular schwannomas, in a young adult is pathognomonic for this diagnosis.
Schwannomatosis
This condition is characterized by multiple schwannomas throughout the body, but is less likely as it typically spares the vestibular nerves which are clearly involved here.
Meningiomatosis
Multiple meningiomas can present as bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses, but schwannomas are more likely given the origin from the internal auditory meatus.
Metastatic Disease
Multiple intracranial lesions in any patient warrant consideration for metastases, although this is less common in this age group and specific location.
Von Hippel-Lindau Disease
This neurocutaneous syndrome can cause multiple CNS tumors, but it typically features hemangioblastomas rather than the bilateral schwannomas suggested by the findings.
eliminated: Sporadic Vestibular Schwannoma
The finding of bilateral masses on MRI rules out a single, sporadic tumor.
Meniere's Disease
This inner ear disorder does not cause bilateral facial weakness or intracranial masses.
Neurofibromatosis type 1
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the defining feature of NF2, not NF1.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2
The presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas and a confirmed NF2 gene mutation is diagnostic for this condition.
Schwannomatosis
This condition is characterized by multiple schwannomas, which aligns with the biopsy findings, though it typically lacks bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Neurofibromatosis type 1
This is the most common neurocutaneous syndrome and a differential for any patient with multiple nerve sheath tumors, although the specific presentation is classic for NF2.
Meningiomatosis
Multiple meningiomas can present with bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses causing similar symptoms and are also associated with NF2.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease
This is another genetic tumor predisposition syndrome that can present with cerebellar tumors causing ataxia and inner ear tumors causing hearing loss.
eliminated: Multiple Sclerosis

Sporadic Vestibular Schwannoma
The presence of bilateral tumors on MRI rules out a single, non-syndromic tumor.
Meniere's Disease
The finding of bilateral intracranial masses rules out this inner ear fluid disorder as the primary cause.

differential: Vestibular Schwannoma
This benign tumor classically presents with slowly progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness due to compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
Meniere's Disease
This inner ear disorder is defined by the triad of vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, which can be progressive over months.
Meningioma
A tumor in the cerebellopontine angle can compress the eighth cranial nerve, producing symptoms identical to a vestibular schwannoma.
Multiple Sclerosis
A demyelinating plaque in the brainstem at the root entry zone of the vestibulocochlear nerve can cause these focal neurological symptoms in a young adult.
Chronic Labyrinthitis
Persistent inflammation of the inner ear could lead to chronic hearing loss, tinnitus, and vestibular dysfunction.
eliminated: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2
The combination of vestibulocochlear symptoms and bilateral facial nerve weakness in a young adult is highly suggestive of bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Vestibular schwannoma

Brainstem glioma
A pontine tumor could directly infiltrate the nuclei of the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves and disrupt cerebellar pathways, causing all the observed signs.
eliminated: Meniere's disease
